title: Christmas Eve

segments.voice: Yesterday, the O Antiphons: old names for Christ sung one a night, each ending with come. Your line was o come, emmanuel.

The church lights go down until the building is almost dark. Up front, someone lights a single taper and turns to the person beside them, who tips an unlit candle into the flame. That person turns to the next. The light walks down the rows, hand to hand, until the whole room glows from below, faces lit as if around a campfire. Then everyone starts to sing, softly, a carol the room seems to know by heart. It's late. Some of the children are asleep on their parents' shoulders.

Why at night? Because the story starts at night. Luke puts the first announcement of the birth not in a palace or a temple, but in a field in the dark: "And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night." Ordinary night-shift workers, awake while everyone else sleeps. An angel appears, the dark lights up, and they are terrified. Then a multitude of angels praises God: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." So churches gather late, some at midnight, some earlier for families with small children, to be awake when the shepherds were. Catholic churches celebrate a Mass at night. Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and others hold candlelight services, and Orthodox churches keep a vigil in their own way, some in January, by the older calendar. And the carol? Tradition tells it like this. A priest in a small Austrian village wrote some verses in German, Stille Nacht, and asked a local musician to set them to music for the Christmas Eve service. They sang it with a guitar. Some tellings add that the church organ was broken that night, but that detail may have been added later. However it began, the song traveled, and its English words became a Christmas Eve fixture: silent night, holy night. It's an odd thing to call that night silent; in Luke it's full of angels. But the song describes the stillness of a sleeping child, and a world that, for a moment, holds its breath.

Sing a carol, any one you know, even just the first verse under your breath, or hum it, or say the words slowly. Then let it go quiet, and sit in the stillness after it. If you pray, you can let the angels' line be your prayer, glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace; if you don't, just rest in the quiet the song leaves.
Christmas Eve. The night before Christmas, kept with late services and carols by candlelight, because Luke's story begins with shepherds awake in the dark.
Your line: silent night, holy night. The shepherds were awake too. Day one thousand ten, by candlelight.

howItsDone: Churches hold services late on Christmas Eve, some at midnight, often with carols and candles passed from person to person; Catholics celebrate Mass during the night, and Orthodox churches keep a vigil, some of them in January by the older Julian calendar.

chat.says: Why do churches hold Christmas services so late at night?
options: Luke's story starts at night, with shepherds awake in a field, so churches keep watch too.
Because the wise men arrived at midnight in Luke, so churches wait up for them.
It's an old rule that worship has to wait until the shops have closed.
chat.meaning: In Luke, the first news of the birth comes to shepherds keeping watch over their flock by night, so churches gather late to be awake when they were.

vigil.meaning: a time of watching and prayer through the night

notes: Claims rule: no year, names or ages for the carol's origin (Joseph Mohr, Franz Gruber, Oberndorf, 1818 are left out); told as 'tradition tells it'.
The broken-organ detail is flagged as possibly later; confirm.
'Silent night, holy night' appears as the carry and in the voice without quotation marks; the English text is public domain but not on the validator's translation list.
Denominational practices (Catholic Mass during the night, candlelight services, Orthodox vigil on their own calendar) are described generally; confirm.
Editor: Luke 2:13 says the heavenly host was 'praising God, and saying', not singing; voice and fork reveal changed to 'praising'. Dropped 'young' for the carol's priest (age not in a cited text).
Editor 2: review line no longer calls the O Antiphon titles 'the prophets' names', since not all come from the prophets (matches the day 1009 fix).

Audit: 'Orthodox churches keep a vigil ... on their own calendar' implied every Orthodox church differs; many (e.g. Greek, Antiochian) keep 25 December. Voice and howItsDone now say some keep it in January by the older calendar.
